cases.name: OPERA's faster-than-light neutrinos
cases.summary: In September 2011 the OPERA collaboration posted a measurement of neutrinos from CERN arriving at Gran Sasso about 60 ns earlier than light would. The collaboration itself asked for scrutiny. The anomaly was traced to equipment faults, including a badly connected fibre-optic cable in the timing chain; the revised analysis, published in JHEP in 2012, found neutrino speeds consistent with the speed of light, as did ICARUS.

record.title: Measurement of the neutrino velocity with the OPERA detector in the CNGS beam

cases.lesson: A large, established collaboration with an excellent track record: the signals here would have been high. The claim was bold and wrong; the method (open scrutiny, independent replication) caught it, not the track record.

record.title: Measurement of the neutrino velocity with the OPERA detector in the CNGS beam

cases.name: BICEP2
cases.summary: In March 2014 BICEP2 reported B-mode polarisation in the cosmic microwave background and interpreted it as evidence of primordial gravitational waves from inflation. It was published in Physical Review Letters in June 2014 with added caveats about dust. A joint BICEP2/Keck/Planck analysis in 2015 found the signal was consistent with polarised Galactic dust; the paper was not retracted.

record.title: Detection of<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:math>-Mode Polarization at Degree Angular Scales by BICEP2
Joint Analysis of BICEP2/ Keck Array and Planck Data

cases.lesson: Published, highly cited and never retracted, yet the headline interpretation did not hold. 'Published' and 'cited' are outcomes this explorer can measure; 'true' is not.

record.title: Detection of B -Mode Polarization at Degree Angular Scales by BICEP2

cases.name: Arsenic-based life
cases.summary: This was a journal paper, not a preprint: Science published it online in December 2010 (print June 2011), claiming a bacterium (GFAJ-1) could substitute arsenic for phosphorus in its DNA. Critics responded quickly, much of it on blogs. Science attached an editor's note (an expression of concern) on 3 June 2011, and in 2012 published two studies (Erb et al.; Reaves et al.) finding GFAJ-1 does not incorporate arsenate into its DNA. Science retracted the paper on 24 July 2025 (Crossref retraction notice 10.1126/science.adu5488), more than 14 years after publication.

record.title: GFAJ-1 Is an Arsenate-Resistant, Phosphate-Dependent Organism
Absence of Detectable Arsenate in DNA from Arsenate-Grown GFAJ-1 Cells

cases.lesson: Peer review and a top journal did not stop a bold claim. For 14 years our outcomes would have scored it a success (published, highly cited, not retracted); the retraction came long after the claim had been refuted in print. Outcomes lag reality, which is why the page says signals are not truth.

record.title: RETRACTED: A Bacterium That Can Grow by Using Arsenic Instead of Phosphorus

cases.name: LK-99
cases.summary: In July 2023 two arXiv preprints claimed LK-99, a copper-doped lead apatite, was a room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductor. Replication attempts worldwide within weeks found no superconductivity; the sharp resistivity drop and partial levitation were explained by copper sulfide (Cu2S) impurities and ferromagnetism.

record.title: Superconductor Pb$_{10-x}$Cu$_x$(PO$_4$)$_6$O showing levitation at room temperature and atmospheric pressure and mechanism
Superionic Phase Transition of Copper(I) Sulfide and Its Implication for Purported Superconductivity of LK-99
LK-99 isn’t a superconductor — how science sleuths solved the mystery

cases.lesson: Small team, bold title ('first room-temperature'), no shared data: the bold-claims flag fires, and the claim failed fast in public. One case does not validate the flag.
